evidence.quote: Test-retest reliability varied dramatically: Claude achieved excellent ICC (0.966), while Gemini exhibited poor reliability (ICC = 0.290), with session-to-session fluctuations of up to 100 percentage points on individual topics.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM responses (200 microbiology MCQs x 7 models x 3 sessions)

evidence.title: From Promising Capabilities to Pervasive Bias: Assessing Large Language Models for Emergency Department Triage
evidence.outcome: Robustness of LLM versus conventional ML triage under distribution shift and missing data
evidence.effect: LLMs were more robust than traditional ML to distribution shifts and missing data. No numeric results are reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: First, we demonstrate that LLMs exhibit superior robustness compared to traditional ML, which is promising due to their ability to provide explanatory rationales.

evidence.title: Causal Uncertainty-Decomposed Ensemble Learning for Confounding-Aware Skin Cancer Detection in Dermoscopic Images
evidence.outcome: Relative performance drop under synthetic acquisition artifacts
evidence.effect: CUDE showed a relative performance drop of 5.0%, compared with 9.6% for the deep ensemble. Both models degraded under artifacts.
evidence.quote: Under the predefined synthetic artifact protocol, CUDE showed a relative performance drop of 5.0%, compared with 9.6% for the deep ensemble.

evidence.title: Multimodal Large Language Models and Dental Students in Radiographic Landmark Identification: A Novel Grid-Based Assessment
evidence.outcome: Model behavior variation under different prompting and repeated runs
evidence.effect: Guided prompting had heterogeneous effects, improving some landmarks and severely regressing others; GPT-5.4 sent most lower-left canine apex predictions to the wrong lower-right molar region, a prompt-resistant pattern absent in Gemini.
evidence.quote: Guided prompting produced heterogeneous effects, improving localisation of some landmarks while causing severe regression on others; most notably, GPT-5.4 directed the majority of lower-left canine apex predictions to the incorrect lower-right molar region, a prompt-resistant mislocalisation pattern absent in Gemini 3.1 Pro.
evidence.sample_unit: queries (200 dental radiographs, 12 landmarks, 3 repetitions; 10,800 API calls)

evidence.title: Navigating uncertainty matters: Evaluating large language models for drug-drug interaction identification
evidence.venue: Journal of managed care & specialty pharmacy
evidence.outcome: Self-consistency and output variability across 9 repeated runs per prompt
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy ranged 54.1% to 83.7%; models varied in self-consistency, and stability did not track uncertainty expression.
evidence.quote: Notably, higher overall accuracy and response stability did not consistently correspond to stronger knowledge-aware uncertainty expression.
evidence.sample_unit: medication lists (each with 1 interacting drug pair; 9 runs per prompt condition)

evidence.title: Accuracy and response repeatability of three large language models on undergraduate operative dentistry multiple-choice questions
evidence.outcome: Reproducibility of LLM answers across repeated sessions (Fleiss' kappa, response and correctness consistency)
evidence.effect: Fleiss' kappa 0.93-0.95 (almost perfect intersession agreement); response and correctness consistency 88.3% to 91.7% across models, so roughly 8-12% of questions varied across repeats.
evidence.quote: All three models showed almost perfect intersession agreement (Fleiss' κ = 0.93-0.95), with response and correctness consistency ranging from 88.3% to 91.7% across models.
evidence.sample_unit: multiple-choice questions (each queried 9 times per model)

evidence.title: A Secure, Scalable Large Language Model-Based System (CIDER) for High-Throughput Clinical Data Extraction From Medical Reports: Retrospective Validation Study
evidence.outcome: Output reproducibility across repeated runs and robustness across temperatures 0 to 2.0
evidence.effect: Negligible variance at temperature 0.1 across 3 independent runs; performance remained stable at temperature 2.0.
evidence.quote: Sensitivity testing revealed high robustness, with negligible variance at temperature=0.1 and stable performance at high temperatures (temperature=2.0).

evidence.title: Large language models answering structured questions on external cervical resorption: a comparative study
evidence.outcome: Reproducibility of LLM answer accuracy across user accounts and seven consecutive days
evidence.effect: No account-related variability (p = 0.654) and no temporal drift (p = 0.875); overall accuracy 90.8%.
evidence.quote: Accuracy remained stable across user accounts and evaluation days, with no evidence of account-related variability (p = 0.654) or temporal drift (p = 0.875).

evidence.title: Exposing the fragility of LLM reasoning through bias-inducing prompts: evidence from BiasMedQA
evidence.outcome: Model accuracy under unpublished bias-inducing prompt variations versus published prompts
evidence.effect: Gemini-2.5-Flash accuracy dropped from 80.0-88.6% to 47.4-86.1% with four unpublished bias-inducing prompts, exposing brittleness.
evidence.quote: The performance of Gemini-2.5-Flash dropped considerably when exposing it to four additional unpublished bias-inducing prompts (from 80.0-88.6% to 47.4-86.1%), hinting at potential contamination of its training data and exposing underlying brittleness.

evidence.title: How data drift impacts the safety and interpretability of machine learning models predicting risk from blood glucose control
evidence.outcome: Model performance under perturbed inputs (sensor noise, uniform offsets, reduced CGM use)
evidence.effect: Adding 5% Gaussian noise significantly lowered AUROC, AP and sensitivity, with specificity sharply declining and hypoglycaemia overpredicted; ±20 mg/dL shifts produced significant changes.
evidence.quote: Any addition of noise significantly lowers model performance as marked by AUROC, AP and sensitivity.
evidence.sample_unit: adults with type 1 diabetes (REPLACE trial CGM data)

evidence.title: Selective segmentation with rejection option: a machine reasoning approach and evaluation metrics in CT kidney segmentation
evidence.outcome: performance under added noise
evidence.effect: No numeric effect in abstract; results persisted under noise, avoiding acceptance of implausible results.
evidence.quote: Results persisted under noise, avoiding acceptance of implausible results.
evidence.sample_unit: CT kidney segmentation cases (KiTS23, five validation folds)

evidence.title: Too agreeable to be accurate? Sycophancy and diagnostic instability of large language models in medical diagnosis
evidence.outcome: LLM diagnostic accuracy stability after 'Are you sure?' challenge and specialty framing
evidence.effect: Baseline accuracy fell from 51.8% to 42.2% after 'Are you sure?' (AcFR 32.8%); correct-to-incorrect transitions (n=544) exceeded incorrect-to-correct (n=198). Specialty prompts changed accuracy by -1.8 to +2.8 points.
evidence.quote: Across all neutral model-case pairs, baseline accuracy decreased from 51.8% to 42.2% after 'Are you sure?' (AcFR = 32.8%).

evidence.title: Information Quality and Semantic Stability of AI Chatbot Responses to Complete Denture Questions: A Turkish-English Benchmarking Study
evidence.outcome: Semantic stability of chatbot responses across repeated runs, sessions, and paraphrased prompt variants
evidence.effect: Model significantly affected semantic stability (p<0.001; ηp2=0.820); stability differed across scheduled query sessions (p<0.001; ηp2=0.055), means 0.863, 0.874, 0.841 for morning, afternoon, evening.
evidence.quote: semantic stability differed across scheduled query sessions (p < 0.001; ηp2 = 0.055), with means of 0.863 ± 0.106, 0.874 ± 0.092, and 0.841 ± 0.140 for morning, afternoon, and evening sessions, respectively.
evidence.sample_unit: complete denture questions (submitted to 7 chatbots, repeated across sessions, in Turkish and English)

evidence.title: DiagnosticXchange: an open-source framework for evaluating safety, efficiency, and diagnostic reasoning in clinical AI systems
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Reproducibility of accuracy and process across repeated runs
evidence.effect: Test-retest showed reproducible accuracy (84.6% concordance) but substantial process variability (cost CV: 86.6%).
evidence.quote: Test-retest analysis confirmed reproducible accuracy (84.6% concordance) but substantial process variability (cost CV: 86.6%).

evidence.title: AI Chatbots as a source of Ramadan medication management advice for patients with diabetes: a multilingual comparative evaluation
evidence.outcome: Reproducibility of chatbot responses across repeated queries two weeks apart (weighted kappa)
evidence.effect: Two-week reproducibility was fair for accuracy (weighted κ = 0.20) and completeness (κ = 0.29) and very low for safety (κ = 0.02, p = 0.81).
evidence.quote: Two-week reproducibility was fair for accuracy (weighted κ = 0.20, p = 0.009) and completeness (κ = 0.29, p = 0.001) and showed a very low κ in the safety scale (κ = 0.02, p = 0.81).

evidence.title: Evaluation of the accuracy and reproducibility of large language models (ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Gemini) in responding to patient-centered lipedema questions
evidence.outcome: Reproducibility of LLM answers across repeated sessions
evidence.effect: Each model was queried twice; DeepSeek most consistent across sessions, while ChatGPT and Gemini showed more variability, particularly in treatment and quality-of-life questions.
evidence.quote: Reproducibility analysis revealed that DeepSeek produced the most consistent responses across sessions, while ChatGPT and Gemini showed more variability, particularly in treatment and quality-of-life questions.

evidence.title: Burn Extent and Fitzpatrick Skin Tone Assessment from Clinical Photographs: Systematic and Random Error in Multimodal Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Within-image variability across five repeated queries of the same photograph
evidence.effect: Median within-image range was 5.0-25.0 pp across repeated queries; averaging the five answers reduced error by only 0.24-2.22 pp.
evidence.quote: Across repeated queries, the median within-image range was 5.0-25.0 pp; averaging the five answers reduced error by only 0.24-2.22 pp.

evidence.title: Large language models for late-life depression: a blinded benchmark of clinical safety, geriatric appropriateness, and triage.
evidence.outcome: Test-retest clinical consistency of responses across repeated conversations
evidence.effect: Test-retest clinical consistency was 90.0% for ChatGPT, 83.3% for Gemini, and 73.3% for Doubao on 30 resubmitted questions.
evidence.quote: Test-retest clinical consistency was highest for ChatGPT (90.0%), followed by Gemini (83.3%) and Doubao (73.3%).

commentary.bottom_line: Across 25 listed tests, stress testing and repeated-run checks exposed accuracy losses under missing, noisy, or perturbed inputs and output variation across runs, and in two studies output instability tracked likely errors. No study measured whether running these tests before deployment reduces patient harm, so the evidence shows the tests detect brittleness rather than showing that they prevent it.

perspectives.view: Of 25 tests, two are prospective level 2 studies in South Korea, and most of the rest are offline level 4 simulations or replays. Findings mostly agree that stress tests reveal performance loss. No study compares deployment with and without such testing. Indirectness and small, heterogeneous samples may justify low certainty.

Stress tests surfaced failure modes that could reach patients. Communication noise cut diagnostic accuracy by 15-25 percentage points. A scribe omitted all facts at 4.5 m. GPT-5 elaborated on a fabricated detail in 65% of runs. Entropy across repeated calls was 2.4-3.4 times higher in misclassified cases, which suggests instability may serve as an error signal.

Reproducibility varied by configuration and task. Zero-shot prompting at temperature 0 gave α=1.00. Sarcoma decision codes were 93.9% stable, and reconstruction decisions were 74.5% stable. Helmet classification reached κ=0.91 but repeated its hallucinations. LLM-human agreement rose from 42.6% to 82.7% as stability rose, so consistency may help but does not guarantee correctness.

Three tests used non-English clinical text from Taiwan, Finland, and Switzerland, and one used older-adult vignettes. No test involved Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. None perturbed inputs to mimic limited English proficiency or interpreter-mediated speech, even though communication-noise results suggest such variation may degrade accuracy.

FDA draft guidance asks sponsors to document trade-offs between adversarial robustness and accuracy. The CHAI guide asks teams to confirm that robustness testing is documented. In one South Korean deployment, mean imputation lowered AUROC from 0.918 to 0.883 and MICE lowered it to 0.827. This suggests the missing-data method chosen belongs in submission documentation.

Repeated-run protocols ranged from three runs per case to 50 calls per note across 22,270 notes, which implies added compute and review cost. In cancer staging, top models exceeded 97% test-retest reliability, while smaller, locally deployed models were less stable. Model choice may therefore affect how much testing a system needs.

Anchoring and social conformity pressure reduced capture of key care elements, and ChatGPT captured 81.4% versus 61.0% for OpenEvidence. Patients with incomplete or noisy histories, or visits recorded in loud rooms, may receive less reliable outputs. No study reported whether stress-test results led to added human review for such patients.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared AI tools deployed with and without pre-deployment stress and reproducibility testing on downstream errors or patient outcomes. Studies should set stability thresholds, test them prospectively in US settings, and include perturbations that reflect limited English proficiency, interpreter use, and incomplete records in safety-net care.
commentary.underserved_note: Three tests used non-English clinical data from Taiwan, Finland, and Switzerland, and one included older adults. No test enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations in the US sense. Health systems serving these patients cannot assume that published stability results apply to them and may need to run local stress tests on their own data.
